slides.title: Adding and Subtracting in Scientific Notation
slides.note: Post the learning target. Say the 'today' line and nothing else yet.

slides.title: Warm-Up
slides.sub: On your own. Four minutes. No notes.
slides.note: Q4 is today's lesson in miniature. 0.49 and 1.2 cannot be added until they are written over the same place value; 4.95 × 10⁴ and 1.21 × 10⁵ cannot be added until they are written over the same power of ten. A board that answers 0.61 lined up the digits instead of the places — that is exactly the student who will add 4.95 and 1.21 today and keep whichever exponent they saw last.

slides.title: Warm-Up
slides.note: Reveal. Ask for the band each question came from only if time allows.

slides.title: Notes
slides.note:
Start from the planets. Neptune is about 4.95 × 10⁴ km across; Saturn is about 1.21 × 10⁵ km. Ask whether the two together are wider than Jupiter (1.43 × 10⁵ km) before anyone computes. Then the two roads: write both in standard form and add, or write both over the same power of ten and add the coefficients. Same number, 170,500 km, both ways. Read 12.1 × 10⁴ out loud as 'twelve point one ten-thousands' — that sentence is why the powers must match.
OFF: 'You can only add things that are the same size. Ten-thousands add to ten-thousands, and the label never changes.'

slides.title: Notes
slides.note:
When the powers already match there is nothing to set up. Add or subtract the coefficients and copy the power of ten down. Then the second line, which is the part students skip: look at the coefficient you ended with. 13 is not less than 10, so the answer is not finished — move the point one place left and raise the exponent by one.
OFF: 'The power of ten is a label. Six thousands plus two thousands is eight thousands — you never add the word thousands.'

slides.title: Notes
slides.note:
Move one number, not both, and move it to match the other. Every place the exponent goes up, the decimal point goes one place left; the number itself never changes. Then the state guide's named wrong answer, written out and killed: a student who adds the coefficients and adds the exponents turns 1,300 + 340,000 into 470,000,000. Ask the class which of the two numbers is anywhere near 4.7 × 10⁸.
OFF: 'The exponents are never added. Adding 10 to the fifth and 10 to the third does not make 10 to the eighth — it does not make a power of ten at all.'

slides.title: Example 1
slides.sub: Same power, and the answer is not finished.
slides.note: SPOKEN ONLY. The powers already match, so ask the harder question first: what will be true about the coefficient when the two are added? (8.6 and 5.9 are each close to 10, so their sum is over 10.)

slides.title: Example 1
slides.note: Add the coefficients, keep 10⁷, then repair. A board with 14.5 × 10⁷ has the right value and an unfinished answer — that is the guide's named misconception and it is worth a full sentence at the board.

slides.title: Your Turn
slides.sub: Same steps, your numbers. Boards up when done.
slides.note: Same shape with negative exponents. Catches 12.3 × 10⁻³ (unfinished) and 1.23 × 10⁻⁴ (point moved the wrong way). 1.23 × 10⁻² is right.

slides.title: Your Turn
slides.note: Reveal; name what a wrong board most likely did (see the note above).

slides.title: Example 2
slides.note: SPOKEN ONLY. Ask which number is easier to move, and why moving the smaller one up is the safer habit — the answer's power of ten is then already the bigger one.

slides.title: Example 2
slides.note: Rewrite 4.5 × 10⁵ over 10⁶ — exponent up one, point one place left — and the subtraction becomes ordinary. A board with 2.8 × 10⁶ or 2.8 × 10¹ subtracted the coefficients without matching first; a board with 6.85 × 10¹ subtracted the exponents.

slides.title: Your Turn
slides.sub: Same steps, your numbers. Boards up when done.
slides.note: The exponents are two apart — the widest gap this benchmark allows. 9.0 × 10⁻⁶ becomes 0.09 × 10⁻⁴. Catches 4.7 × 10⁻⁴ (the point moved one place too few, so 0.9 came off instead of 0.09) and 5.51 × 10⁻⁶ (wrong power kept).

slides.title: Your Turn
slides.note: Reveal; name what a wrong board most likely did (see the note above).

slides.title: Whiteboards   ·   Question 4 of 9
slides.note: The repair in the other direction: a coefficient below 1 is also unfinished. Point one place right, exponent down one. A board holding 0.7 × 10⁸ has done the subtraction and stopped one step early.

slides.title: Whiteboards   ·   Question 6 of 9
slides.note: Diagnostic. B and A have the same value, and the question asks for the form — that is the whole point. If the room splits between A and B, sixty seconds and a re-vote before you reveal.

slides.title: Whiteboards   ·   Question 7 of 9
slides.note: Negative exponents, one apart. Moving up from 10⁻³ to 10⁻² takes the point one place left, so 6.4 becomes 0.64. A board with 1.4 × 10⁻² never matched the powers.

slides.title: Whiteboards   ·   Question 8 of 9
slides.note: Working backwards, and it forces the repair to be read in reverse: the finished answer has to be un-finished before the blank can be filled. A board with −3.48 subtracted 4.5 from 1.02.

slides.title: Whiteboards   ·   Question 8 of 9

slides.title: Whiteboards   ·   Question 9 of 9
slides.sub: Take your time. Boards up when you have written it.
slides.note: Written, and it is the exit evidence. Full credit needs all three pieces: he added the coefficients without first writing both over the same power of ten; he added the exponents, which is never done; and the sum is 3.413 × 10⁵. A student who names only one mistake has half the item. 'He added wrong' names neither.

slides.title: Independent Set
slides.sub: Six questions. On your own, in silence.
slides.note: Hand out the Independent Set. Silent work. Circulate and mark what you see; do not teach. Whatever is not finished goes home.
